{{Short description|Concept in Scholastic philosophy}}
[[File:AlbertusMagnus.jpg|thumb|upright=0.9|Saint Albert the Great]]

In [[Scholasticism|scholastic philosophy]], the '''aevum''' (also called '''aeviternity''') is the [[Time|temporal]] mode of existence experienced by [[angel]]s and by the [[saint]]s in [[heaven]]. In some ways, it is a state that logically lies between the [[eternity]] (timelessness) of [[God]] and the temporal experience of [[Matter (philosophy)|material beings]]. It is sometimes referred to as "improper eternity"<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Anzulewicz |first=Henryk |date=2001-06-21 |editor-last=Porro |editor-first=Pasquale |title=Aeternitas - Aevum - Tempus: The Concept of Time in the System of Albert the Great |url=https://brill.com/display/book/edcoll/9789004453197/B9789004453197_s006.xml |journal=The Medieval Concept of Time |doi=10.1163/9789004453197_006 |isbn=9789004453197|url-access=subscription }}</ref> or "participated eternity".<ref name=":1" />

== Etymology ==
The word ''aevum'' is [[Latin]], originally signifying "age", "[[aion (deity)|aeon]]", or "everlasting time".<ref>Charlton T. Lewis and Charles Short, ''[[A Latin Dictionary]]'' (Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1879), 64–65.</ref> It comes from the Greek term "αἰών" meaning eternity in the atemporal sense.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Porro |first=Pasquale |date=2001-06-21 |title=Angelic Measures: Aevum and Discrete Time |url=https://brill.com/display/book/edcoll/9789004453197/B9789004453197_s007.xml |journal=The Medieval Concept of Time |publisher=[[Brill Publishers]] |doi=10.1163/9789004453197_007 |isbn=9789004453197|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Before the 13th century, the term ''aevum'' was used synonymously with eternity.<ref name=":1" /> The word ''aeviternity'' comes from the [[Medieval Latin]] [[neologism]] ''aeviternitas''.{{Citation needed|date=March 2025}}
 
== History ==
Both [[Plato]] and [[Aristotle]] recognized two modes of duration: Time and Eternity.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Steel |first=Carlos |date=2001-06-21 |editor-last=Porro |editor-first=Pasquale |title=The Neoplatonic Doctrine of Time and Eternity and its Influence on Medieval Philosophy |url=https://brill.com/display/book/edcoll/9789004453197/B9789004453197_s003.xml |journal=The Medieval Concept of Time |doi=10.1163/9789004453197_003 |isbn=9789004453197|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Plato said that the soul must be in time while Aristotle said that the soul must be in eternity.<ref name=":0" /> The [[Neoplatonism|Neoplatonist]] philosopher [[Simplicius of Cilicia]], said there must be a third mode to describe celestial bodies and souls which are everlasting but still change.<ref name=":0" />

In his [[exegesis]] of the [[Book of Genesis]], [[Augustine of Hippo]] also recognized a mode of duration distinct from time and eternity. In Augustine's view, Heaven and earth, taken to mean formless matter, were created before time, and thus had existence in a participated eternity.<ref name=":1" />

In the beginning of the 13th century, independently of direct influence from Simplicius, a doctrine of three measures of duration was developing at the [[University of Paris]].<ref name=":0" /> These were known as eternity, sempiternity (or perpetuity), and time.<ref name=":0" /> In the [[Summa]] attributed to [[Alexander of Hales]], this middle measure of duration was used to describe angels, souls, and celestial spheres, all of which have a beginning but no end.<ref name=":0" />

The concept of the aevum, using the term as distinct from eternity, dates back at least to [[Albertus Magnus]]'s first systematic study of time, ''De quattuor coaequaevis''.<ref name=":2" /> In contrast to the concept of sempiternity, Albertus notes that even if something has no beginning and no end, its mode of duration would be distinct from the eternity of God.<ref name=":0" /> To Albertus, eternity is pure [[Potentiality and actuality|actuality]] while aevum is always actual, but only the actuality of some potency.<ref name=":0" />

A description of aevum is found in the ''[[Summa Theologica|Summa theologica]]'' of [[Thomas Aquinas]]. Aquinas identifies the aevum as the measure of the existence of beings that "recede less from permanence of being, forasmuch as their being neither consists in change, nor is the subject of change; nevertheless they have change annexed to them either actually, or potentially". As examples, he cites the [[Classical planet|heavenly bodies]] (which, in medieval science, were considered changeless in their nature, though variable in their position.<ref name=":0" />) and the angels, which "have an unchangeable being as regards their nature with changeableness as regards choice".<ref>[[Thomas Aquinas]], ''[[Summa Theologica]]'', First Part, Question 10, Article 5. [https://www.newadvent.org/summa/1010.htm#article5]</ref>

At the end of the 13th century, in ''De mensuris'', [[Theodoric of Freiberg]], further developed the philosophy of time. Theodoric distinguishes five measures of duration: <ref name=":0" />

# Superaetenitas - the measure of divine being; beyond eternity 
# Aeternitas - the measure of the being of divine intelligences "if such beings exist"
# Aevum - the measure of angelic beings, which have a beginning, an everlasting existence, with no change in their substance but change in their accidents
# Aeviternitas - the measure of celestial bodies, which have a beginning and are everlasting but inferior in perfection to angels
# Time - the measure of beings with limited period of existence

In the 14th century, both [[Berthold of Moosburg]] and [[William of Ockham]] rejected the concept of aevum. Berthold held that there were only two measures of duration: eternity and time.<ref name=":0" /> William did not even believe eternity could be properly called a measure and held that time was the only measure of duration.<ref name=":0" />

== Contemporary philosophy ==
[[Frank Sheed]], in his book ''Theology and Sanity'', said that the aevum is also the measure of existence for the saints in heaven: {{blockquote|"Aeviternity is the proper sphere of every created spirit, and therefore of the human soul... At death, [the body's] distracting relation to matter's time ceases to affect the soul, so that it can experience its proper aeviternity."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sheed |first=Frank |title=Theology and Sanity |date= |publisher=[[Ignatius Press]] |year=1993 |isbn=978-1684221004 |edition=2nd}}</ref>}}
